clinicalPearls: Amebiasis is infection with Entamoeba histolytica, an intestinal protozoan; ~90% of infections are asymptomatic cyst passage and only ~10% are invasive (p.1753).

Symptomatic amebic colitis develops 2-6 weeks after ingestion of infectious cysts, with gradual-onset lower abdominal pain and mild diarrhea progressing to malaise, weight loss, and dysentery (p.1755).
In full-blown dysentery patients may pass 10-12 stools per day consisting mainly of blood and mucus with little fecal material; virtually all have heme-positive stools (p.1755).
In contrast to bacterial diarrhea, fewer than 40% of patients with amebic dysentery are febrile and stools show a paucity of neutrophils (p.1755).
Cecal involvement may mimic acute appendicitis (p.1755).

Definitive diagnosis of amebic colitis requires demonstration of hematophagous (erythrocyte-ingesting) trophozoites of E. histolytica; this is the only way microscopy can identify the species (p.1756).

Because trophozoites are rapidly killed by water, drying, or barium, at least three fresh stool specimens should be examined; wet mounts, iodine-stained concentrates, and trichrome-stained preparations confirm diagnosis in 75-95% of cases (p.1756).

Stool antigen detection (Gal/GalNAc lectin EIA, sensitivity 87%, specificity >90%) and multiplex PCR (sensitivity/specificity approaching 100%) are more sensitive, specific, and rapid than microscopy (p.1757).

Serology (ELISA) is positive in >90% of cases of colitis, ameboma, or liver abscess; results usually revert to negative within 6-12 months, so positivity with a compatible syndrome suggests active disease (p.1756).

E. histolytica infection is widespread in the Indian subcontinent, Africa, parts of East Asia, and Central/South America, often affecting children under 5 in areas of poor sanitation; in developed countries returning travelers, immigrants, MSM, military personnel, and institutional inmates are the main at-risk groups (p.1753).
Invasive amebiasis does not elicit eosinophilia (p.1757).
harrison.pathophysiology: E. histolytica is acquired by ingesting viable cysts from fecally contaminated water, food, or hands (food-borne exposure being most common). Motile trophozoites excyst in the small intestine; in most patients they remain as harmless commensals in the large bowel and re-encyst, shedding infectious cysts in stool. In some patients trophozoites invade the colonic mucosa (causing colitis) or enter the portal bloodstream (causing distant abscesses, most often hepatic). Trophozoites attach to colonic mucus and epithelium via the Gal/GalNAc adherence lectin and release glycosidases, proteases, and cysteine proteinases that degrade mucus, collagen, elastin, immunoglobulins, and complement anaphylatoxins; mucosal damage follows via contact-dependent cytotoxicity (apoptosis, trogocytosis, lysis of inflammatory and epithelial cells) and contact-independent mechanisms (inflammatory mediators such as prostaglandin E2). Resistance to reactive oxygen/nitrogen species and to complement-mediated lysis are virulence factors. The earliest lesions are mucosal microulcerations of the cecum, sigmoid, or rectum; submucosal extension beneath viable surface mucosa produces the classic 'flask-shaped' ulcer with trophozoites at the margins. Human infection is notable for a paucity of inflammatory cells (in part because trophozoites kill neutrophils) (p.1753-1755).
additionalDifferentials: Bacterial dysentery / inflammatory diarrhea (Campylobacter, enteroinvasive E. coli, Shigella, Salmonella, Vibrio)
Inflammatory bowel disease (ulcerative colitis, Crohn disease)
Carcinoma of the colon (especially when an ameboma mass is present)
nonInfectiousMimics: Inflammatory bowel disease (ulcerative colitis / Crohn disease)
Colonic carcinoma (mimicked by ameboma on barium studies)
additionalInvestigations: Examination of at least three fresh stool specimens (wet mount, iodine-stained concentrate, trichrome-stained preparation) for cysts/trophozoites
Stool test for occult blood (heme) and microscopy for neutrophils
Stool antigen detection assay (monoclonal anti-Gal/GalNAc lectin enzyme immunoassay)
Stool multiplex PCR / nucleic acid amplification for GI protozoa
Serology (ELISA / indirect hemagglutination) for invasive amebiasis
Sigmoidoscopy with biopsy of the edge of ulcers if stool studies negative (avoid in fulminant colitis)
Biopsy of a colonic mass to confirm ameboma and exclude carcinoma
Stool culture for bacterial pathogens to exclude bacterial dysentery
redFlags: Fulminant intestinal infection with severe abdominal pain, high fever, and profuse diarrhea (rare; predominantly in children)
Toxic megacolon with severe bowel dilation and intramural air
Patients receiving glucocorticoids are at risk for severe amebiasis
harrison.prognosis: Outcome relates to the clinical syndrome: about 90% of infections are asymptomatic and self-limited, and uncomplicated amebic colitis responds well to therapy with ulcers characteristically healing with little or no scarring. Fulminant colitis, toxic megacolon, and perforation are rare but carry a poor prognosis. Treated colitis generally resolves, but severe disease (notably in those given glucocorticoids or in children with fulminant infection) markedly worsens outcome (p.1755-1756).
pitfalls: E. histolytica cannot be distinguished microscopically from the non-pathogenic commensal E. dispar (nor from E. moshkovskii or E. bangladeshi); most asymptomatic carriers actually harbor E. dispar, which is incapable of invasive disease and does not warrant treatment, so species-specific antigen detection or PCR is needed (p.1754, p.1756).
Cysts must also be differentiated from non-pathogenic Entamoeba hartmanni, Entamoeba coli, and Endolimax nana, which do not cause disease (p.1756).

Amebiasis must be excluded before starting glucocorticoid therapy for suspected inflammatory bowel disease; unsuspected amebiasis treated with steroids can precipitate severe colitis or toxic megacolon (p.1755-1757).
An ameboma can be mistaken for cancer on barium studies; positive serology or biopsy can prevent unnecessary surgery (p.1755).
Sigmoidoscopy/biopsy and barium studies are dangerous during fulminant or acute colitis because of the risk of perforation (p.1756-1757).
Trophozoites are rapidly killed by water, drying, and barium and may be confused with neutrophils, so examination must use multiple fresh specimens with experienced microscopy (p.1756).
harrison.severityClassification: Harrison describes a clinical spectrum rather than a formal grading scheme: (1) asymptomatic cyst passage (~90% of infections); (2) symptomatic amebic colitis/dysentery with bloody mucoid stools; and (3) rare fulminant intestinal infection (severe pain, high fever, profuse diarrhea, predominantly in children) that may progress to toxic megacolon, full-thickness necrosis, or perforation (p.1753, p.1755).
